questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given a Description of the Radius and Angle
questions.problem: Given that the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $8,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${150}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, what are the Cartesian coordinates of $P?$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ where

$$
r=8,\,\theta ={150}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡({150}^{∘}) \\  & =8(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡({150}^{∘}) \\  & =8\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-4\sqrt{3},4).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Using a Diagram
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13992889/assets/6e9d2238ca77532c3adda8d35f94061d108c3e15432ce48fdc33885ddf4f4e48.png)

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(5,\frac{7\pi }{6})$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{5\pi }{6},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(5,\frac{7\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=5.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $5,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $5.$

Notice that one must traverse the circle clockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{7\pi }{6},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{7\pi }{6}-\frac{5\pi }{6}=\frac{\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(5,\frac{\pi }{3})$

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3}) \\  & =5\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\  & =\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(\frac{5}{2},\frac{5\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Cartesian Coordinates of a Point Given Some Information About Another Point
questions.problem: The point $A$ has polar coordinates $(r,\frac{5\pi }{6})$ and the point $B$ has polar coordinates $({r}^{2},\frac{11\pi }{6}).$ Find the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ given that the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ are $(-3,\sqrt{3}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we use the Cartesian coordinates of $A$ to find $r,$ the distance between $A$ and the origin:

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, the polar coordinates of $B$ are

$$
((\sqrt{12})^{2},\frac{11\pi }{6})=(12,\frac{11\pi }{6}).
$$

 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =12\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6}) \\  & =12(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =6\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{11\pi }{6}) \\  & =12(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(6\sqrt{3},-6).$

The diagram above shows a circle of radius $r$ centered at the origin. If the polar coordinates of the point $A$ are $(6,\frac{\pi }{6})$ and $m∠AOB=\frac{\pi }{2},$ what are the Cartesian coordinates of $B?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, since $A$ has polar coordinates $(6,\frac{\pi }{6}),$ we must have $r=6.$ Also, since the points $A$ and $B$ both lie on a circle of radius $6,$ the $r$-coordinate of $B$ must also be $6.$ 

Notice that one must traverse the circle counterclockwise to move from the point $A$ to point $B.$ Since the $\theta $-coordinate of $A$ is $\frac{\pi }{6},$ the $\theta $-coordinate of $B$ must be

$$
{\theta }_{B}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{2\pi }{3}.
$$

So, the polar coordinates of $B$ are $(6,\frac{2\pi }{3})$ 

Now, we convert $B$ to Cartesian coordinates. To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =6(-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =6(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =3\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(-3,3\sqrt{3}).$

questions.problem:
If the distance from a point $P$ to the origin is $3,$ and that $P$ makes an angle of ${240}^{∘}$ with the positive $x$-axis, then the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are$\,(${{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}}$).$
questions.worked_solution:
We notice that the point $P$ is described using polar coordinates $(r,\theta )$, where

$$
r=3,\,\theta ={240}^{∘}.
$$

To convert from polar coordinates to Cartesian coordinates, we use

$$
x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

First, we calculate the $x$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡({240}^{∘}) \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the $y$-coordinate of $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =3\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡({240}^{∘}) \\  & =3\cdot (-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Cartesian coordinates of $P$ are $(-\frac{3}{2},-\frac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}).$
